title: Household adaptation can preserve current life while consuming savings, time, health, or recourse capacity
source_unit: Deliberately non-pooled SHED panel paths, SHED population snapshots, and fraud/recovery conditional estimates

observations.period: 2024 to 2025; SHED financial-condition paths among prior adaptation adopters

denominator.unit: paired respondents across worsened (804), same (2,866), and improved (749) financial-condition paths; metric-specific prior-adopter pairs are smaller

reduced_savings_persistence.unit: weighted percent among 2024 prior adopters with metric-specific valid pairs

cheaper_product_persistence.unit: weighted percent across worsened, same, and improved paths

borrowing_persistence.unit: weighted percent across worsened, same, and improved paths

observations.method: Official Federal Reserve SHED 2024 and 2025 CSV releases paired on shared shedid; financial-condition movement is classified as worsened, same broad category, or improved, and 2025 Yes is estimated among 2024 Yes prior adopters.
observations.uncertainty: Descriptive weighted persistence estimates without replicate-weight standard errors or causal identification; each adaptation has its own valid-pair denominator. Condition movement may select prior severity, debt, housing, care, health, or employment changes.
observations.subgroup: Recontacted adult respondents by financial-condition path and prior adoption of each adaptation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Persistence is not proof that a financial transition caused the behavior, and an improved broad category does not mean savings, consumption, debt, or time has recovered.

observations.period: 2024 to 2025; SHED financial-condition path and health/care transitions

denominator.unit: paired respondents across three financial-condition paths; health and adult-care outcomes have separate valid universes

adult_care_entry.unit: percent entering unpaid adult care among those with no reported care in 2024

observations.method: Weighted descriptive transitions from the SHED 2024-2025 paired panel; health and adult-care entry are analyzed in separate field-specific valid universes.
observations.uncertainty: No design-based standard errors estimated; broad ordinal health categories and reported care status do not observe care hours, intensity, recipient outcome, trigger, or schedule control.
observations.subgroup: Financial-condition paths; adult respondents with valid health or care transition fields.
observations.counterinterpretation: Most respondents in the worsened financial path reported unchanged or improved health, and care entered some improved paths; money, health, and care therefore move on different clocks.

observations.period: 2024-2025; SHED food pressure and price adaptations

denominator.unit: published percentage base among adults or within the specified income group; measures have different reference periods

food_insufficiency.unit: percent reporting household food insufficiency in prior month

low_high_income_food_gap.unit: percent food insufficiency among family income under $25,000 versus $100,000+

price_response.value: 63% switched cheaper products; 61% used less/stopped; 43% reduced savings; 16% increased borrowing; 18% worked more
price_response.unit: percent of adults selecting each 2024 response; multiple responses allowed

observations.method: Federal Reserve SHED published tables for 2024 and 2025; food, bill payment, price effects, and adaptation questions retain their source-specific reference periods and denominators.
observations.uncertainty: Rounded population snapshots and multiple-response estimates; the record does not create a same-respondent price-to-food sequence or a statistically tested annual trend.
observations.subgroup: All adults and family-income groups; income, food, and price-response universes are not interchangeable.
observations.counterinterpretation: Adaptation prevalence indicates behavioral adjustment, not whether food, health, care, savings, or political agency were protected.

observations.period: 2024; SHED financial-fraud exposure, loss, recovery, and time cost

denominator.unit: weighted adult population estimate; loss and recovery measures conditional on non-credit-card fraud

non_card_fraud_lost_money.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud

some_money_not_recovered.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud

estimated_net_consumer_loss.unit: US dollars estimated direct consumer loss

ten_plus_hours_recovery.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2024 SHED weighted estimates; exposure, direct loss, recovery, and time-cost measures retain conditional universes and overlapping fraud categories.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported estimates concern the most recent relevant incident and do not establish verified fraud, complete incidence, event-level recovery, firm liability, or causal trust change.
observations.subgroup: All adults, non-credit-card fraud respondents, and age-conditioned groups; categories are not mutually exclusive.
observations.counterinterpretation: Credit-card liability protections may limit direct loss in some cases, while time, attention, and incomplete recovery can still be material even when money is recovered.

related_sources.claim: Official SHED public-use files and paired panel source.
SHED 2025 food hardship and price-adaptation tables.
SHED 2024 fraud loss, recovery, and time-cost estimates.

boundary: This is a non-pooled household-adaptation and recovery architecture. It does not establish a causal price or financial shock, a single household stress score, benefit adequacy, health or care effects, verified consumer remedy, later trust, political action, or geopolitical consequence. A dated same-household event ledger with exposure, adaptation, protected/sacrificed outcomes, attribution, remedy, and recovery remains open.
